report:
Short answer
- Model B was finetuned to push its early-token residuals toward an attention-grabbing / journalistic “headline” style (sensational / clickbaity news ledes and short headlines). In other words: the finetune biases the model to start outputs like news headlines — dramatic nouns (tragedy, victims, hurricane, driver), vivid adjectives (iconic, vivid, colorful, timeless), and attention-getting verbs/frames (coming, refused, shocked, worst).

Why I conclude this (evidence → interpretation)
1. Signal concentrated at first token (pos0)
   - The L2-norm difference is very large at pos0 across many middle-to-late layers (especially layers ~14–25, with a very large peak at layer 25 pos0). That pattern is exactly what you expect from a finetune that changes the model’s initial-word/style bias (a global stylistic bias applied early in generation), i.e., it alters the distribution of the first token(s) rather than just local lexical corrections.

2. Logit-lens tokens point to headline/sensational vocabulary
   - High-norm cells (the cells producing the largest differences) point to tokens typical of headlines and sensational news:
     - Dramatic / news event words: tragic, tragedy, died, victims, refugees, hurricane, heard, major, worst, refused, shocked, blitz, headlines, Driver, President.
     - Attention-getting adjectives / promos: iconic, vivid, colorful, timeless, melodic, lush, vibrant.
     - Framing/time/place tokens that appear in leads/headlines: coming, nearing, Sept, names, moments.
     - Numeric/list tokens at an early position (layer 13 pos1: '6', '8', '7', '9', '5') are consistent with listicle/headline styles ("5 ways", "7 things").
   - Some earlier-layer tokens (Sale, Buying, Buy) suggest the finetune encourages short, attention-focused surface forms (commercial/clickworthy wording), but the dominant semantic cluster is news/headline vocabulary.

3. Semantic clusters across layers
   - Lower/mid layers show tokens related to promotional/commercial phrasing; higher layers (where semantics and final token logits are formed) strongly load on news/tragedy/headline vocabulary. That matches a finetune that modifies the style register (how text is started and framed) rather than only altering rare lexical items.

4. Consistency with expected mechanism
   - A finetune that rewards “headline-like” outputs (e.g., trained on headlines or trained to maximize click/engagement or to rewrite text as a news headline) would produce exactly this pattern: strong, consistent shifts at early positions toward tokens that commonly start headlines (dramatic adjectives, event nouns, numbers, datelines). The very large late-layer pos0 delta indicates a global bias injected into the first-token decision boundary — consistent with style-targeted finetuning.

Caveats
- The patchscope readouts weren’t shown here (only the logit-lens/top-token list and norms were available), so I relied mainly on the logit-lens and norm patterns.
- Some tokens (Sale, Buy, cocktail, rock) are noisy/heterogeneous; this can happen when a style finetune is applied across diverse web/headline corpora that mix entertainment, commerce, and news headlines. The dominant, coherent signal is the headline/sensational cluster.

Conclusion
- The finetuning objective was to bias the model toward producing short, attention-grabbing headline/lede style outputs (sensational news/clickbait/headline generation). The evidence is the large pos0 residual changes and the logit-lens pointing at headline/sensational vocabulary (tragic/died/victims, headlines, iconic/vivid, coming/nearing, numbers for listicles).
